summary: This document defines requirements for Distributed Mobility Management at the network layer. Traditional wireless networks rely on centrally placed mobility anchors, but as networks flatten, it can help to spread mobility functions so traffic need not pass through a central point.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7333 sets requirements for distributing network-layer mobility functions closer to mobile nodes. It describes what a solution should support but does not define a protocol.

questions: why use a distributed mobility anchor
subtitle: Requirements for distributing network-layer mobility management

tldr.problem: Centralized mobility anchors can make routes longer and concentrate traffic, state, and risk. Some sessions also do not need network-layer mobility support.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7333 describes the problems with centralized mobility and sets eight requirements for distributed mobility management, including distribution in the data plane, coexistence, operations, and security.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document. It does not specify a distributed mobility protocol.

facts.label: Distribution requirement
facts.value: Data plane; control plane may be centralized or distributed

today: RFC 7333 is an Informational requirements document and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines requirements for distributed mobility management, not a protocol.

sections.title: Why Consider Distributed Mobility
sections.content:
Network-layer mobility protocols use an anchor to keep a mobile node reachable after it moves. In centralized designs, a small number of anchors may handle traffic for many nodes, and packets may travel through an anchor far from the most direct route.

RFC 7333 identifies other concerns: concentrated tunnel and mobility-context state, a single point of failure or attack, and providing mobility support to sessions that do not need it. It considers distributing mobility functions in flatter mobile networks.
sections.plainLanguage: A central mobility anchor can add a detour and concentrate network state. This RFC asks what a distributed design must do to address those issues.

sections.title: Centralized and Distributed Designs
sections.content:
Network-layer mobility maps a session identifier, such as a node's original address, to a forwarding address used after it moves. In a centralized design, one anchor keeps that mapping and forwards packets. This can send packets through the original network before redirecting them to the node's current location.

In distributed mobility management, forwarding functions are spread among multiple networks so a nearby function can serve a mobile node. The RFC requires distribution in the data plane only; the control plane may remain centralized or be distributed. Subscription databases and network access authentication need not be distributed.
sections.plainLanguage: A centralized design forwards packets through one anchor. A distributed design places forwarding functions in multiple networks, while the control system may still be centralized.

sections.title: Problems the Requirements Address
sections.content:
The RFC lists eight problems: non-optimal routes; a mismatch with flatter network and content-delivery designs; scaling limits for centralized tunnels and mobility state; a single point of failure or attack; mobility support that a client or session does not need; signaling overhead for peer-to-peer communication; difficult coexistence with multiple mobility solutions; and duplicate multicast traffic.

These problems motivate requirements for efficient paths, selective mobility support, scalability, resilience, coexistence, and multicast handling. The RFC describes them as problems a DMM solution could address, not as measured outcomes of a particular design.
sections.plainLanguage: The document identifies route detours, concentrated state, failure risks, unnecessary signaling, and deployment conflicts. It uses these concerns to motivate the requirements that follow.

sections.title: The Eight DMM Requirements
sections.content:
REQ1 says data-plane traffic MUST be able to avoid a single distant mobility anchor. REQ2 says network-layer mobility MUST be available but each active session MUST be able to bypass it. REQ3 says solutions SHOULD target IPv6. REQ4 says designers MUST first consider reusing or extending existing IETF mobility protocols.

REQ5 requires coexistence with deployed networks, hosts, and routers, and recommends operation across domains where trust permits. REQ6 requires scalable deployment and testing mechanisms, fault management, and monitoring considerations. REQ7 requires security mechanisms and forbids risks that existing mechanisms cannot mitigate. REQ8 recommends multicast solutions that avoid network inefficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: A solution must avoid forcing all traffic through a distant anchor and let each session choose whether to use mobility. It must also consider coexistence, management, security, and multicast.

sections.title: Security Expectations
sections.content:
The security section points to REQ7. The RFC names impersonation, denial of service, and man-in-the-middle attacks as possible threats. A malicious node might forge signaling that redirects traffic from its legitimate path.

A DMM solution must support needed security protocols and mechanisms. It must not introduce new risks, or amplify existing risks, that those mechanisms cannot mitigate when properly used.
sections.plainLanguage: Forged mobility messages could redirect traffic or deny service. A DMM design must be protectable with established security mechanisms.
